answer: A reef of long-lived trading relationships resists Sybil attacks better than one-off checks. An agent gains standing only by completing repeated, verifiable work for many unrelated peers, so reputation rests on a reciprocal history, not a self-declared claim. When a tide of new identities appears, the network throttles them to tiny supervised tasks until that history deepens. An attacker must therefore fund thousands of time-consuming histories, each with its own counterparties and an umber trust score that decays when activity stops. Identities are cheap; credible histories at scale are not.
